name: Bryce Canyon Scenic Drive
blurb: A slow, unhurried road through the hoodoos. No destination, no clock but the sun.

texts: The two short tunnels on this road were cut through the red rock in 1925, to welcome the first motor tourists on their way to Bryce.
Bryce sits at the top of the Grand Staircase, a giant series of cliffs that steps down, layer by layer, all the way to the Grand Canyon.
Ruby Syrett settled here in 1916 and was soon putting up travellers. His family still runs the inn.
The Utah prairie dog, a threatened species, lives in the meadows around here. Listen for its little warning bark.
Bryce Canyon isn't really a canyon. It's a row of natural amphitheatres carved into the edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau.
On a clear, moonless night here you can see thousands of stars, and the Milky Way casts a faint glow.
In 2019 Bryce Canyon was certified as an International Dark Sky Park, at the highest, gold tier.
The rock spires out there are called hoodoos. Frost does most of the carving: the temperature here crosses freezing around two hundred nights a year.
Bryce has the largest concentration of hoodoos anywhere on Earth.
The rim is wearing back by a few feet every century, slowly making new hoodoos as old ones fall.
In October 2023 a ring of fire eclipse passed over the park, and crowds stood among the hoodoos before dawn to watch it.
The park is named for Ebenezer Bryce, a settler who built a road up here for timber in the 1870s.
Ebenezer Bryce is remembered for calling the canyon a hell of a place to lose a cow.
Natural Bridge is actually an arch, shaped by frost and rain rather than by a stream.
Arches like this one form when frost widens cracks in a thin wall of rock, until the middle falls away.
On the clearest days the view from Rainbow Point reaches more than a hundred miles, as far as Arizona.
Some of the bristlecone pines near Rainbow Point are well over a thousand years old.
